performers: Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra; Wilhelm Furtwängler, conductor
intro: Wilhelm Furtwängler conducted the Berlin Philharmonic in this recording of the finale, Adagio lamentoso, of Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 6 in B minor “Pathétique”, Op. 74, made in Berlin in 1938. The falling violin melody passes from one section to the other, and the movement ends on a low B in the double basses.

sections.label: A · Lament divided between violins, Adagio lamentoso
sections.mNote: First and second violins exchange notes of the lament.

sections.label: B · Broad D major theme, strings
sections.mNote: The strings play a descending melody above the horns.

sections.label: C · Opening lament returns, B minor
sections.mNote: The strings play the B minor melody again.

sections.label: D · Lament theme returns, strings and brass
sections.mNote: The lament theme returns and expands to the final climax.

sections.label: E · F♯ and the low brass
sections.mNote: The dominant dies away towards the quiet brass chorale.

sections.label: Coda · Second theme over low B, B minor
sections.mNote: The second theme returns above a low B in the basses.

cues.title: Opening melody, divided violins
cues.text: The first and second violins share the falling melody, alternating one note at a time. Neither section’s part forms the tune on the page. Combined, the two parts make a continuous line above the opening half-diminished chord.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 16, reproduces the violin parts. Opening harmony: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Vladimir Davydov, 1893
cues.text: In February 1893 Tchaikovsky wrote to Vladimir Davydov about the planned finale: “a long drawn-out adagio”. He was delighted with the new symphony and intended to keep its programme secret.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Vladimir Davydov, letter 4865, 11/23 February 1893. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Andante theme in D major
cues.text: The Andante has a broad melody in D major. First violins and violas play it above the horns, and trombones reply. The melody moves downwards.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the Andante scoring; D-major key at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The opening lament returns in the strings in B minor. Tchaikovsky extends its falling phrases across the orchestra and builds again from the melody that began the movement.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the opening theme’s return and expansion. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final climax over an F♯ pedal
cues.text: Strings and brass play the returning lament up to its last climax. Beneath the agitated melody the bass holds F♯, the dominant of B minor, before the music begins its long decline.
cues.evidence: Finale’s late climax and F♯ pedal: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Jurgenson, 30 October 1893
cues.text: On 30 October 1893, two days after he conducted the première in Saint Petersburg, Tchaikovsky wrote to his publisher Jurgenson. He said the symphony had caused bewilderment, but “I’m more proud of it than any of my other works”.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Pyotr Jurgenson, letter 5062, 18/30 October 1893. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Final return in B minor
cues.text: The broad melody returns for the last time in B minor. Muted strings descend above a repeated low B in the double basses. In the closing pages the texture thins and more of the music passes to the cellos and basses.
cues.evidence: Final return in B minor and muted strings: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Low-B pulse and thinning close: https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
